paragraphs.heading: A cold current off South America
paragraphs.text: The Humboldt Current, which people also know as the Peru Current, is a cold ocean current with low salt content that flows north along the west coast of South America. It is an eastern boundary current heading toward the equator, and it reaches 500–1,000 km (310–620 mi) out from the shore. It stretches from southern Chile, near 45° south, to northern Peru, near 4° south. There its cold, upwelled water runs into warm tropical water and forms a boundary called the Equatorial Front.

paragraphs.heading: Whose name it carries
paragraphs.text: The current is named for the German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt. Yet José de Acosta had found it 250 years before Humboldt did. In 1846 Humboldt published measurements of the cold current in his book Cosmos.

paragraphs.heading: Cold sea, dry land
paragraphs.text: Off Peru, near 5° south, the sea surface can be as cold as 16 °C (61 °F). That is very unusual for the tropics, where most waters are warmer than 25 °C (77 °F). The current cools the climate of Chile, Peru and Ecuador. It is also largely behind the dryness of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, of coastal Peru and of southern Ecuador. The current chills the sea air, and cool air like this makes clouds and fog but little rain.

paragraphs.heading: How it flows
paragraphs.text: The trade winds are the main force driving the current. It moves through the upper ocean toward the equator, carrying fresh, cold Sub-Antarctic surface water north along the outer edge of the subtropical gyre. In southern Peru most of the flow turns away from the coast, while a weaker branch keeps heading toward the equator. Around 18° south, the cold, fresh water starts to mix with warm, salty Subtropical Surface water.

paragraphs.heading: A sea full of fish
paragraphs.text: Upwelling lifts nutrients to the surface, where they feed phytoplankton and raise the output of life. The Humboldt is the most productive of all eastern boundary current systems, providing roughly 18-20% of the world's marine fish catch, mostly sardines, anchovies and jack mackerel. Its wealth also feeds other fisheries, marine mammals such as eared seals and cetaceans, and seabirds. From time to time the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) interrupts the upwelling, often with large social and economic costs.

paragraphs.heading: A layer short of oxygen
paragraphs.text: Where part of the current swings away from the coast of Peru, the water is less well ventilated. This is the main cause of an intense oxygen minimum zone, or OMZ, that sits from just below the surface down to middle depths. Among the permanent hypoxic zones of the world's oceans, it ranks fourth in size, and its core lies off Peru, with a shallow upper boundary that spans depths of roughly 100 m (330 ft) to 600 m (2,000 ft). The sinking and decay of material made by primary production also adds to it. As a result, many creatures are forced to stay near the surface, where they can get oxygen and nutrients, while the OMZ shelters organisms able to live in hypoxic conditions.
